channel.title: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
channel.description: Phys.org internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: New study: The last bird to go extinct in NZ has lessons for saving other species
item.description: The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972.

item.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy
item.description: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity, floods, heat waves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one.

item.title: NEPTUNE poised to replace Navy's global weather model, improving forecasts over open ocean
item.description: The U.S. Naval Research Laboratory-developed Navy Environmental Prediction sysTem Utilizing a Nonhydrostatic Engine, known as NEPTUNE, is poised to become an operational Navy weather prediction capability, providing improved environmental forecasts to support naval operations around the globe.

item.title: Putting Google's AI hurricane model to the test
item.description: A week before Hurricane Melissa slammed into Jamaica last fall, the forecast models couldn't agree on where it was headed or how strong it would get. One got it right—an AI model from Google DeepMind, which called both the storm's path and its Category 5 strength.

item.title: AI companions could help reduce loneliness, study finds
item.description: AI companions could help reduce loneliness by creating a greater sense of belonging and improving self-esteem, according to new research from Durham University Business School.

item.title: Q&A: Making hydrogen peroxide without using precious metals
item.description: Hydrogen peroxide is used in many industrial processes, with several million tons of it being manufactured worldwide every year. Whereas the standard production method requires rare precious metals, chemists from Rutgers University–Newark in the US and the University of Bonn have now described an alternative technique that does away with these metals, making it potentially cheaper and more sustainable. Their findings have now been published in the journal Nature Communications. In the following interview, the authors describe the technology.

item.title: Can AI save peer review from AI?
item.description: Academic journals are flooded with papers. At publishing giant Elsevier, the number of submissions rose 56% in just three years—from 2.7 million in 2022 to 4.2 million in 2025. That's a lot more papers. And peer reviewers, who generally volunteer their time, were already stretched thin.

item.title: Mercury-bound X-ray telescope delivers first images after eight years in space
item.description: The first data from a U.K.-built instrument heading to Mercury have provided observations of one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky from aboard the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo spacecraft in the inner solar system.

item.title: 'PAC-MAN' capsules that gobble up particles in turbulent water show promise for filtration and drug delivery
item.description: Scientists have created hollow capsules with single openings that can selectively filter particles thanks to the turbulence in surrounding waters—at times, ingesting particles like PAC-MAN eating up dots.

item.title: Britain should treat healthy seas as essential infrastructure, say scientists
item.description: Researchers are calling for lasting investment in healthy seas to support food security, protect coastlines and strengthen economic resilience.

item.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
item.description: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question.

item.title: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses is off to a strong start
item.description: If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

item.title: Staying alive in marsh muck: The tiny 'snorkels' cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
item.description: Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available.

item.title: Dual-purpose polymer dots could combine bioimaging and light-triggered cell death in one material
item.description: A research team led by professor Youhei Takeda at the University of Osaka, in collaboration with professor Zachary M. Hudson at the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Canada, has developed a polymer material that combines fluorescent cell imaging with the potential to kill cancer cells when activated by light. The material could offer a simpler approach to developing "nanotheranostic" technologies, which bring disease imaging and treatment together in a single platform.

item.title: Individual meerkats are ace solo navigators
item.description: After meerkats emerge each morning from their burrow to warm in the early sun, there's one thing on their collective mind, and that's to find food. They navigate communally as they head off, working slowly along their route before returning home swiftly at the end of the day. But although the tight-knit band navigates as one, some members of the clan could be more experienced after roaming solo, shaping the community's maneuvers.

item.title: How microbes make drug-like chemicals without damaging themselves
item.description: University of Michigan researchers have discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug-like molecules—compounds that can fight infections or kill cancer cells—without damaging themselves.

item.title: ESA's Hera probe uses 'superhuman' vision to inspect NASA's asteroid crash site
item.description: Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour (13,700 miles per hour). However, we still don't know just how much of a success it actually was—DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up.

item.title: If tiny 'primordial' black holes exist, here's how we might find them
item.description: Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter—the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's matter.

item.title: The snake with a built-in egg peeler
item.description: Dr. Arthur Tiutenko from FAU and colleagues from LMU München and the South African National Museum in Bloemfontein discovered a new species of snake in the Harenna Forest, on the southern slopes of Ethiopia's Bale Mountains: Dasypeltis albigularis, or the white-throated egg-eater. "Three other new species in this genus are still waiting in line," the zoologist adds.

item.title: How a tiny chemical mark on a protein can be placed to double gene activity
item.description: Tiny chemical marks on histones—the proteins that package our DNA—can profoundly influence gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence. One such mark, known as histone acetylation, plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and is frequently disrupted in diseases such as cancer. Researchers, however, wondered how the enzymes responsible for adding these marks know exactly where to place them.

item.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
item.description: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks.

item.title: Light-activated nanoparticles may help treat head and neck cancer
item.description: For patients with head and neck cancer, treatment can come at a high cost to their quality of life, affecting their ability to speak, swallow and even breathe due to invasive procedures. Now, Penn State researchers have developed a light-activated nanoparticle system with the long-term goal of shrinking tumors while limiting exposure to healthy tissue and improving patients' quality of life after cancer treatment. Penn State has licensed the technology to Illuminate Therapeutics, which is advancing its preclinical development.

item.title: Ethiopian volcano's mysterious methane outburst may have a culprit—magma that never erupted
item.description: Experts were puzzled when satellite observations showed a volcano in Ethiopia emitting huge quantities of methane despite not erupting, but a team of researchers led by the University of Bristol believe they have discovered why this happened—and their findings could have implications for historical climate change research.

item.title: Ahead of Giving Tuesday, study finds charitable giving often misses communities with greatest need
item.description: As Giving Tuesday approaches, a recent study led by a University of Massachusetts Amherst public policy researcher finds that communities with greater economic disadvantage typically see less private charitable giving—despite having greater needs in many cases.

item.title: Gene variant gives male malaria mosquitoes a mating edge in the heat
item.description: Mosquitoes play a major role in spreading malaria, and understanding how they adapt to climate change is important for improving malaria prevention and control.

item.title: Cichlid sibling rivalry: Young fish fight more in some species than others
item.description: Though we may fight with our siblings sometimes, for most people a sibling is a constant companion throughout childhood and often for one's entire life. Yet this is not always the case in the animal kingdom: in some species, siblings engage in serious fights that can even escalate to fratricide. They may be genetically related, but must also compete for limited resources.

item.title: Rethinking the 'girls are worse with money' myth
item.description: New research led by Dr. Stephen Agnew from Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury's (UC) Department of Economics and Finance is challenging one of the most persistent assumptions in education and everyday culture: that teenage girls are less financially literate than boys.

item.title: Remote jobs diminish hiring bias against mothers
item.description: The "motherhood penalty"—a workplace bias that assumes mothers are less committed to their careers, resulting in fewer opportunities, lower pay and slower advancement—could be reduced by shifting jobs from in-person to remote, according to new research by Claire Daviss, assistant professor of organizational behavior at the ILR School.

item.title: Optical DNA mapping assembles yeast genomes at chromosome scale
item.description: Large, complex genomes remain difficult to characterize accurately, even with modern DNA sequencing. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology have now extended an optical genome mapping approach, previously demonstrated for bacterial genomes, to more complex eukaryotic genomes. Using two yeast species, they generated optical maps covering entire chromosomes, including large repetitive regions that are particularly difficult to reconstruct.

item.title: Improving hydrogen production from water can support abundant global crops
item.description: Water, at least in its purest form, contains hydrogen and oxygen. In 1800, scientists first used electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen gases. Today, this process, known as water electrolysis, is widely used to produce hydrogen for industrial purposes, including manufacturing ammonia for agricultural fertilizers that sustain global food production.
